title: Star Crumbs for Hazel and Pip
markdown:
The sky was a lovely deep purple. The sun yawned a big sleepy yawn and went to rest behind the soft rolling hills. Hazel the hedgehog, whose little bits were as soft as flower buds and never felt pokey, and Pip the penguin, who walked with a happy rolling thump-thump-thump, spread a big soft rug in the quiet meadow. The rug shimmered like a sleepy moonbeam. On it they had crumbly moon cheese that tasted like the softest cloud, and dewdrop juice that shone in the dimming light.

As they nibbled and sipped, tiny shimmering flecks fell from their treats, like little fallen stars.

“Oh, look,” chirped Pip, flippers moving with quiet bubbly joy. “Star crumbs. Little bits of sleepy sky.”

Hazel laughed softly, like leaves in a mild breeze. “Little bits of nighttime magic. So sparkly.” A few more fell onto the rug and caught the last of the sun.

The mild breeze whispered through the tall sleepy grass, a hushed tune. The first shy stars peeked in the velvety sky. The air smelled of clover and flowers just beginning to bow. Hazel and Pip watched, noses wiggling, as the sky filled with twinkling lights, each one winking a soft hello.

“When the meal is done,” said Hazel, voice as calm as a quiet pond, “and we fold our rug, we must tuck the star crumbs in, nice and neat, so they can rest too. Even little bits of night need their slumber.”

“Yes,” agreed Pip, dark eyes shining. “Gentle star tidiers. Softest paws and smooth tummies.”

With slow mindful movements, Hazel gathered the tiny crumbs. Her gentle paws nudged them across the moonbeam rug. Brush, brush, brush went her soft fur against the weave, coaxing sparkles into small sleepy piles. Pip slid his sleek tummy along the rug like a little boat on a calm sea, helping the last bits join the heap.

“Hush now, little stars,” he whispered, a low rumbly penguin voice like distant waves. “Time for rest. Time to snuggle down.”

They worked together, slow as a lullaby sung very softly. Each crumb was treated like a precious jewel. One tried to hide in a fold; Hazel unfolded it as if turning a page. Another hid under a sliver of moon cheese; Pip ate the cheese first, very carefully, and rescued the sparkle. He breathed on a stubborn fleck and it rolled, polite as a marble, into the pile. A third crumb sat on Hazel’s nose until she sneezed it, gently, onto the heap. The last star crumb nestled in a tiny twinkling heap in the centre of the rug.

Above them the sky was a deep dark velvet cloak, dotted with a million real bright stars, all twinkling goodnight wishes down. Hazel felt warm from nose to tail. Pip snuggled closer on the rug.

“All tidy,” murmured Hazel, counting the heap once more with her eyes.

“All snug,” echoed Pip, tummy still moonbeam-warm.

Crickets chirped like tiny fiddles playing a sleepy tune. The wind murmured in the leaves. The moon, now fully awake, cast a peaceful silvery glow over the meadow. Hazel and Pip lay looking up, eyes wide, then heavy, eyelids like little pillows. They yawned little yawns. Wrapped in their moonbeam rug, with cricket-song for a lullaby, they drifted into sweet starry dreams, the tidy heap of crumbs shining once, then settling, as if night had been tucked in too.
